body:
@jdussouillez Hi, this issue is probably invalid, though I'll leave it up the experts in the CC list. Are you aware of any tools, browsers, which will auto replay a verb with the side-effects like `POST` in response to the redirect request ? 

My own take on it is that if the browser can't POST in the auto-redirect then the Java client emulating the browser should not either. 

AFAIK, POSTs are only propagated as part of the redirect if an HTML page is returned, with 200, but the page contains a form submit action on the completion of its load,
Thanks

I agree with @sberyozkin.

@FroMage do you have any input on this as well?

@sberyozkin Yeah I understand, and trust me I know it's not great. Unfortunately some online services work like this. And Postman, cURL and other API tools handle this so I wondered if it was a bug or a by-design choice.

Feel free to close this issue if you don't want to implement it.

---

An IRL example: Microsoft require this to [get an API token for some Dynamics 365 plugins](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/inventory/inventory-visibility-api#inventory-visibility-authentication).

> The https://securityservice.operations365.dynamics.com/token URL is a general URL for the security service. When you call the URL, the first response is an http redirect response with the status code 307 in the response headers, and an entry with the key "Location" that contains the target URL for the security service.

Workarounds are possible (the simplest one: not using the REST client for this particular API call).

> cURL and other API tools handle this so I wondered if it was a bug or a by-design choice

It was probably not intentional. We can certainly have a look
Thanks for the explanation. We'll have a look and see what can be done

I was curious about what the RFCs said but nothing on 307 responses. But I found some details on the 302 code. It seems the POST/302/GET is the classic way to do it. But X/307/X is not against the RFC. *I'm no expert in HTTP RFCs so please correct me if I'm wrong*

In old [RFC 2616](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-10.3.3) :

> 302 Found
> [...]
> Note: [RFC 1945](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1945) and [RFC 2068](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2068) specify that the client is not allowed to change the method on the redirected request.  However, most existing user agent implementations treat 302 as if it were a 303 response, performing a GET on the Location field-value regardless of the original request method. The status codes 303 and 307 have been added for servers that wish to make unambiguously clear which kind of reaction is expected of the client.

----

In [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-302-found) :

> 302 Found
> [...]
> Note: For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request. If this behavior is undesired, the [307 (Temporary Redirect)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.307) status code can be used instead.

Hi @jdussouillez Thanks for the clarification

>Workarounds are possible (the simplest one: not using the REST client for this particular API call).

Catching a redirect exception and retrying with a new location in the catch block can be a reasonable solution. Auto-redirects for POSTs would be neat if Georgios and others agree on it, though might require some extra security support around it (ex, a large file is read and posted but 30x arrives).
